**Verdict:** Yes. Admit the real flaws your prospects already complain about, state each one first, and then make the claim you want believed. Hormozi calls this a "damaging admission" and says it's possibly his favorite tactic.

**Based on:** said it (Hormozi addressed this directly, in the copywriting leaves on damaging admissions and proof and authority)

**Why he'd say it**
- Trust beats promise: "what you'll sacrifice in promise you'll gain in trust and trust trumps promise" ([[yt-JDR-R--4HhM]] @ 13:09, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JDR-R--4HhM&t=789s)
- Find the complaints and claim them: "write down all of the flaws all the things that people complain about the things that you know you could do better and claim them" ([[yt-JDR-R--4HhM]] @ 15:03, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JDR-R--4HhM&t=903s)
- The structure is "true, damaging thing *but* the claim": "the statement that comes after the word but is the part that is the thing you want them to believe" ([[yt-JDR-R--4HhM]] @ 13:44, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JDR-R--4HhM&t=824s)
- His own example: "our websites are ugly as hell but they convert" ([[yt-JDR-R--4HhM]] @ 15:03)
- Admitting flaws also filters buyers: "Listen, before I tell you about the good, let me tell you about the bad." Then "So then they can self-qualify." ([[yt-MH-IMJxbUY4]] @ 19:42 and 20:14)
- Use humor if you can: "if you can do with humor you get even more bonus points" ([[yt-JDR-R--4HhM]] @ 15:39)

**How to word it** (my application of his structure, not his wording)
- "Our [flaw prospects already mention], but [the outcome they actually buy]."
- "It's [unpolished / slower / more expensive / not for everyone], but [the result it delivers]."
- "Honest answer: we're not the cheapest. We're the one [specific result]."
- Pick flaws that don't touch the core promise. His "ugly as hell but they convert" admits something cosmetic that doesn't affect results. Admitting a flaw that breaks the outcome you sell is a different case, and the vault doesn't cover it.

**What would change his answer**
- If the flaw is one a buyer would hit in the first week and the ad hides it, the trust gain won't cover the refund and churn. The vault has no direct case for this. The closest is his retention material, where he says overwhelm and bad fit drive churn ([[business/retention/overwhelm-and-onboarding]]).
- He pairs admissions with proof. Expect him to want the flaw followed by documented results, not a bare confession ([[marketing/copywriting/proof-and-authority]]).
- He says "tell the truth" to stand out in a crowded market. If your market isn't crowded, the case for admitting weaknesses is weaker.

**Caveat:** The "research" that admitting a bias builds belief is unnamed, and the Eminem rap-battle story is an illustration. Neither is his own data ([[marketing/copywriting/damaging-admissions]]).

**Verdict:** Hormozi's benchmark is about 80% monthly retention (roughly 20% monthly churn) as typical. Below 70% retention (over 30% churn), he says retention is the highest-ROI lever and you should fix it before anything else. Don't judge the number by itself: he says churn falls steeply with tenure, so the real question is whether people get past day 90 and month six.

**Based on:** said it (Skool platform data, in a single video)

**Why he'd say it**
- The benchmark and worry line: "if less than seven out of 10 people want to stay on a monthly basis, you probably need to work on your retention more than anything else. It'll be the highest ROI lever." ([[yt--j8_YCWZ05Q]] @ 1:39; https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-j8_YCWZ05Q&t=99s)
- Tenure matters most: "the biggest rule is that churn drops dramatically with time." Churn falls to around 10% or less after 90 days, then to about 2% by month six. ([[yt--j8_YCWZ05Q]] @ 3:19 and 3:53; https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-j8_YCWZ05Q&t=199s)
- Reframe the goal: "How do I get someone to stay past day 90? How do I get these people to stay past month six?" He says not to overhaul the business over a bad month-one churn number. ([[yt--j8_YCWZ05Q]] @ 4:24; https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-j8_YCWZ05Q&t=264s)
- Why it matters: "halving churn doubles lifetime value," not just a 10–12% boost. ([[yt--j8_YCWZ05Q]] @ 2:13)
- Overwhelm is a churn driver: "all we did is we gave them more reason to cancel because they never used it." ([[yt--j8_YCWZ05Q]] @ 10:54)
- Showing up matters: "if a member feels like the owner isn't active or doesn't care, they leave." ([[yt--j8_YCWZ05Q]] @ 13:39)

**Caveats on the numbers**
- The vault's retention page says "under 10% churn as best," but I couldn't find that as a direct quote. The "10% or less" figure in the source is the churn rate after day 90, not an overall target. Don't use "under 10% monthly" as his benchmark.
- He says a community or subscription under 90 days old will show inflated churn, because no one has reached the low-churn months yet. Judge a new community on its tenure curve, not its first-month churn.
- The data comes from Skool, a platform he promotes. The vault flags this as a blind spot. Treat the exact numbers as Skool-specific.

**How to apply it (what he'd do):** Track joins against cancels every month. Split churn by tenure: month one to three, then day 90, then month six. For cancellers, ask why they left. Keep the offer to one or two things members value most, and get them a quick win in their first 24 hours.

**Beyond the vault:** The vault doesn't say whether 20% monthly churn is good for your community in general, or whether your product resembles Skool's. Check your numbers against your own tenure curve before treating his benchmark as a target.

**What would change his answer:** If your product is high-ticket, has few users, or sits in a category where cancellation is a normal part of the model, his 80% benchmark may not apply. He says the Skool averages don't fit insurance premiums or alarm systems.

**Verdict:** Pay it off. Hormozi would put the debt ahead of growth cash. He says he skews "very close to the Ramsey side" on debt, and his advice is to get out of the hole first, then take risk. The exception is spending that has a measured return, which he would keep funding.

**Based on:** follows from what they said (confidence: high)

**How we get there**
1. He was asked about the same situation. A consulting client had $60,000 of business debt, and Hormozi endorsed a plan to pay it off in four to five months. He kept "continue to pay off the debt" second on the priority list, behind only a 10% price raise ([[yt-OQf2Ba-Lp_4]] @ 30:45, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OQf2Ba-Lp_4&t=1845s).
2. The rule behind it: "The first step is that we have to cut all costs, so that we can take more risk." and "get yourself out of the hole as fast as humanly possible." ([[yt-jfW6gL6hKhk]] @ 0:32; [[yt-XGm2ERU9qtA]] @ 17:53, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XGm2ERU9qtA&t=1073s). Risk is only worth taking once you have time and cash, and debt is a claim on that cash.
3. Your situation fits that rule: a profitable business with $60k of debt and cash that is your only room to take risk.

**Why they'd say it**
- Debt is a risk that compounds: "Risk when multiplied over a long time horizon tends to come due." ([[yt-OQf2Ba-Lp_4]] @ 9:10, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OQf2Ba-Lp_4&t=550s). He adds that "businesses have seasons, they have volatility," and points to debt-free companies such as Chick-fil-A.
- He frames paying down debt as partly emotional: "I'd say this is more of an emotional thing, but it's just this back of mind thing." ([[yt-OQf2Ba-Lp_4]] @ 8:37). That makes the relief itself part of the payoff.
- His growth rule is "spend as much as humanly possible while maintaining break even or better," provided ROAS and CAC hold ([[yt-tGhe3sBuk34]] @ 8:17; [[yt-OQf2Ba-Lp_4]] @ 10:48). Keep cash for growth only when a channel is already paying back, measurably and predictably.

**What they've done:** He endorsed the $60k paydown above and does not describe borrowing to grow in his own business.

**What would change their answer:** If the debt is cheap and you have a channel with proven, measured returns above the debt's cost, he would keep spending on that channel. The inference breaks if the cash is needed to keep ads running, or if you have no proven channel and the cash is your only growth fund.

**Where the vault is thin and where it conflicts**
- The vault never compares interest rates. A 4% loan and a 25% card are different decisions, and he doesn't address that.
- His own view is in tension: in 2026-06 he describes heavy debt as how fund managers get rich, a month after the Ramsey-leaning view ([[tensions]]). He doesn't reconcile the two. The fund example is a round-number illustration, not evidence about small operators.
- The $60k match is useful, but it's one consult about business debt, not a general rule.

**My own take (not in the vault):** I'd split the decision by interest rate. Pay off anything above roughly your expected return on growth spend, and keep cash for growth if you have a channel with a known return above the rate. Keep a cash buffer for slow months first, since he would want you out of the hole before taking risk.

Want me to save this as `derived/pay-off-debt-or-grow.md`?

**Verdict:** No. Don't hold prices to protect the close rate. Hormozi would raise them, starting with about 10%, and watch the close rate weekly. He would say you're underpriced: at an 82% close rate, you have room to charge more.

He'd put it bluntly: "They're so afraid of charging money that they actually sell themselves out of a sale." His reasoning is that a higher price raises the customer's confidence that you can deliver, so for a normal service it can lift the close rate, not hurt it. He also says that as long as the close rate stays above break-even, the raise makes more money.

**Based on:** said it (confidence: high). He addressed almost this exact case in a May 2026 consult with the owners of ProShine, an HVAC duct-cleaning company doing about $1.25M a year. The leaf is [[pricing/premium-pricing/raising-prices-to-close-more]].

**How we get there**
1. The nearest case: he said "whenever I hear 80% or over 80% close rates, I usually know that there's room in sale," and told ProShine that a 10% raise was "more asking than telling" as long as they "close more than 65%" ([[yt-OQf2Ba-Lp_4]] @ 8:06, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OQf2Ba-Lp_4&t=486s). ProShine had already raised prices 23% after their first consult, and he recommended another 10% (about $1,650 per unit).
2. The rule behind it, from his thinking page: charge more to the people who value it most, and treat an 80%+ close rate as proof the price is too low ([[thinking/hormozi]]).
3. Your case matches: an 82% close rate, a $1.2M HVAC service business, and a price you're considering holding. So he'd say raise it.

**Why they'd say it**
- Raising price increases trust in delivery: "if you raise your price, you increase the emotional investment, you increase the perceived value, you increase the results, and you decrease the demandingness of the customer" ([[yt-OQf2Ba-Lp_4]] @ 7:33, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OQf2Ba-Lp_4&t=453s).
- Pricing is one of the biggest levers for a business your size: "some of the biggest levers that exist in the business is simply charging more because people actually believe you can deliver the service now" ([[yt-OQf2Ba-Lp_4]] @ 8:06).
- The "keep prices so we don't lose the close rate" fear is the mistake he describes. His claim is limited to normal services, not luxury goods ([[pricing/premium-pricing/raising-prices-to-close-more]]).

**What would change their answer**
- The close rate falls below break-even. He ties the decision to a threshold, so run the break-even before you raise. His 65% figure assumes variable cost per job is about 62% of price. Your 38% is a net margin, which already includes fixed costs, so use contribution margin per job instead. If variable costs are a smaller share of price, break-even moves up (roughly 68% at 50%). My arithmetic, not from the vault.
- Caveat on the evidence: the 65% and 23% figures come from one consult, and the ProShine follow-up numbers are projections. The principle is his, but the proof is thin.
- Ignore price objections from people who aren't your ideal customer. He says price works as a filter there ([[business/retention/price-objections-and-annual-plans]]).

If you want, I can save this as `derived/keep-prices-or-raise.md`.

**Verdict:** Hormozi says a banker told him that moving his company's listing from a European exchange to the NASDAQ would make the same business worth four times as much. That idea led him to his current focus: marketing and storytelling for companies about to IPO. He then took an equity deal with a pre-IPO company for about nine to twelve months of work, worth roughly $7–8 million on IPO day.

**Based on:** said it. This is from the Diary of a CEO interview (April 2023), which the vault compiled into the profile. No wiki page covers this story, so I'm citing the raw transcript. The transcript is auto-captioned, so the exact figures are approximate.

**Why he tells it**
- The four-times claim: "when my company went public on a Stock Exchange in um Europe… we were having the meetings with the banks… we went on this road show met 20 different investment Banks we considering an IPO um in another country they told me that our business would be worth four times more if it was just on a different stock market if you move it to the NASDAQ the exact same business would be worth four times more" ([yt-x3e73Qn6NOo @ 1:34:12](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=5652s))
- The lesson he draws: "I thought about that a couple of years later when I was thinking about the skill set that I had acquired… I looked for an industry where my skill set was in least Supply but highest demand and return the greatest and it turned out that industry in terms of social media marketing and storytelling I felt was most in demand" ([@ 1:34:43](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=5683s))
- Why storytelling pays pre-IPO: "if you're going to IPO if you have a good story it can swing your valuation by hundreds of millions" ([@ 1:35:17](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=5717s))

**The equity deal**
- The company was not his own. It was "the first company I worked with," which he says IPO'd at about $3 billion (the caption is garbled here, so treat that figure as rough).
- He was paid a fee of about $10,000 for the freelance marketing work, and took equity "as part of an equity deal," which he says was worth about $7–8 million on IPO day, for "nine months work… basically freelance" ([@ 1:35:51](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=5751s)). I read the caption "take 7 million" as the equity value; the "$10,000" figure is my reading of "a th000 bucks," so check the audio if you need the exact number.
- He contrasts this with a local gym paying about $10,000 for the same skills: "I could go help a local gym and get paid a th000 bucks or I could go help a company that was in the leadup to an IPO… and take 7 million" ([@ 1:35:17](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=5717s)).
- That reasoning led to his current company, which he calls "flight story" in the captions. It applies the same skills to industries that can pay more, starting with the IPO market and then biotech. He said it had about 100 people at the time of the interview.

**What would change his answer:** He is describing a past event, so the figures are his own recollection. The four-times claim is a banker's pitch he repeats, not a verified valuation. Within the vault, nothing contradicts it. The sources don't say how the equity was later realized.

If you want this kept, I can file it as `derived/` or compile the story into the wiki (for example under `business/`).

**Verdict:** He didn't. The vault has no case where Hormozi told a roofing owner to stop door-knocking and move budget into Google Ads. In the one roofing consult that covers door-knocking, he told the owner to go all in on door-to-door.

**Based on:** said it (the opposite of the premise). I didn't find "Google Ads" anywhere in the Keys Roofing transcript, and no vault page links Google Ads to that advice.

**What he said:** In the "Scale or Fail" consult with Caleb, owner of Keys Roofing in St. Louis (two months old, about $20K a month from door-knocking and referrals), Hormozi's reasoning was:
- "I want to focus all efforts on the highest return stuff that you can do right now." ([yt-o64cI6tebnU @ 3:16](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=o64cI6tebnU&t=196s))
- "Now I think that in terms of scale, you should go all in door to door." ([@ 9:49](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=o64cI6tebnU&t=589s))
- "It's what you're good at." ([@ 10:21](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=o64cI6tebnU&t=621s))
- He framed reps' commission per door knocked, e.g. "Just knock that many doors." ([@ 10:54](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=o64cI6tebnU&t=654s))

The vault's reasoning: with limited time and money, put everything behind the highest-return channel the owner is already good at, and scale it with a door-to-door team rather than new channels. Caveats: the $10-per-door figure is his illustration, and the 90-day revenue figures are the guest's own.

**Other roofing advice from the same consult (not about ads):** a VSL before the sales call ([[sales/closing/vsl-before-the-sale]]), a maintenance membership credited $2 for every $1 toward future repairs ([[business/business-models/maintenance-memberships]]), and a menu upsell ([[sales/closing/menu-upsell]]).

**Where ads do come up:** Hormozi's paid-ads advice in the vault is about creative, landing pages and scaling proven returns, mostly for other businesses. Those pages don't mention roofing or door-knocking. See [[marketing/advertising/_overview]] and [[marketing/funnels/ad-landing-pages]].

**What would change this answer:** a source in which he tells a roofing owner to drop door-knocking. The vault doesn't have one. If you have a clip with that advice in mind, add it and I'll check it against the transcript.
